title: Lok Sabha Passes Bill Recognizing Digital Bank Records as Court Evidence
excerpt: The Bankers' Books Evidence Bill 2026 replaces a 135-year-old colonial-era law, giving electronic banking records full legal standing in Indian courts for the first time.
body:
• The Lok Sabha passed the Bankers' Books Evidence Bill 2026 by voice vote on August 5, updating a 135-year-old law to recognize digital and virtual bank records as admissible court evidence.
  • Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman moved the bill, which replaces the Bankers' Books Evidence Act of 1891 and creates a technology-neutral legal framework for financial records in Indian courts.
  • The bill passed without debate amid opposition disruptions over student examination irregularities; the Lok Sabha was adjourned for the day shortly after.
  • The legislation may be extended to cover records from non-banking financial companies, payment aggregators, and fintech platforms, broadening its reach beyond traditional banks.

A Law From 1891 Gets a Digital Overhaul

India's Parliament took a quiet but consequential step on Tuesday when the Lok Sabha passed the Bankers' Books Evidence Bill 2026, replacing a colonial-era statute that has governed how banking records are treated in court for over a century.

https://x.com/moneycontrolcom/status/2084620851643888039

The original Bankers' Books Evidence Act of 1891 was drafted in an era of handwritten ledgers and physical account books. While amendments over the decades had grafted some digital provisions onto the old law, the patchwork approach left significant gaps as Indian banking moved almost entirely online.

The new bill, introduced by the government on August 3 and moved for passage by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, provides explicit legal recognition for digital and virtual bank records. Electronic statements, online transaction logs, digital payment receipts, and records generated by core banking systems will now carry the same evidentiary weight as physical books of account.

What the Bill Changes

At its core, the legislation creates a technology-neutral framework for banking evidence. Rather than tying admissibility to specific storage media—paper, microfilm, magnetic tape, as the old law did through successive amendments—the new bill defines admissible records in functional terms. Any record generated, stored, or transmitted by a banking institution in the ordinary course of business qualifies, regardless of the underlying technology.

This matters because India's banking infrastructure has changed beyond recognition since the last major amendments to the 1891 Act. The Unified Payments Interface processed over 16 billion transactions in a single month earlier this year. Neo-banking platforms, payment wallets, and decentralized finance applications handle billions more. Courts have increasingly encountered disputes involving digital-native financial records that sat awkwardly within the old evidentiary framework.

The government has signalled that the law may be extended beyond traditional banks to cover non-banking financial companies, payment aggregators, and fintech platforms, though the specific scope of any extension will depend on subsequent notifications.

Passed Without Debate

The bill's passage was procedurally swift but politically unremarkable. Opposition members continued protests over alleged irregularities in student examinations, shouting slogans that drowned out legislative proceedings. The bill was passed by voice vote without floor debate, and the Lok Sabha was adjourned for the day shortly afterward.

The lack of discussion drew limited attention partly because the bill is technical and largely uncontroversial—few legislators oppose modernizing evidence laws for digital banking. But legal practitioners have noted that certain provisions, particularly around the certification and authentication of digital records, will require careful implementation to prevent misuse.

Implications for the Legal System

Indian courts have long grappled with the admissibility of electronic evidence. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, which replaced the Indian Evidence Act in 2023, expanded the definition of admissible documents to include electronic records. But the interaction between that law and the ageing Bankers' Books Evidence Act created interpretive ambiguity, particularly around whether bank-generated digital records required separate certification under Section 63 of the new evidence code.

The Bankers' Books Evidence Bill 2026 resolves this overlap by providing a dedicated, updated statutory pathway for banking records. Lawyers handling commercial disputes, loan recovery cases, and financial fraud prosecutions will no longer need to navigate competing provisions across multiple statutes.

What It Means for NRIs

For Indians abroad, the change is directly relevant. NRIs frequently maintain accounts with Indian banks that are managed entirely online. Disputes over NRI fixed deposits, property-linked loans, and cross-border remittances have historically faced evidentiary challenges when digital records were the only documentation available. The new law ensures those records are admissible on their own terms, without requiring conversion to physical formats or additional certification hurdles that added cost and delay.

Looking Ahead

The bill will now move to the Rajya Sabha for consideration during the current Monsoon Session. Given the absence of significant political opposition to its substance, passage in the upper house is expected to be straightforward. The larger question is implementation: how quickly courts, banks, and financial regulators align their practices with the new framework, and whether the government follows through on extending the law to fintech platforms that operate outside traditional banking regulation.
